title: Deploy with systemd, Nginx and HTTPS on a VPS
summary: Run a private application process behind Nginx, with managed startup, HTTPS and distinct deployment checks.

sources.title: Engineering Digest: How to Host Spring Boot on VPS: Production Guide (2026)
Spring Boot: traditional deployment and proxy configuration

richText: What runs on the server
A virtual private server (VPS) gives you a Linux machine to manage. You maintain the operating system, Java runtime, application process, proxy, network rules and logs.
Build the JAR outside the server when possible, then deploy that known artifact. Use the Java version supported by the application’s Spring Boot release.
Run the application as a dedicated user with access only to its required files. Bind its HTTP port to 127.0.0.1 when Nginx is the public entry point.
systemd manages the process, restarts it after failure when configured, and starts it at boot. Running java in an interactive terminal is not a process-management plan.

# /etc/systemd/system/journal.service
[Unit]
Description=Journal application
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=journal
WorkingDirectory=/opt/journal
EnvironmentFile=/etc/journal.env
ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -jar /opt/journal/journal.jar
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
Configuration and logs
Create the user, deploy directory, JAR and environment file before starting the unit. The example assumes those files exist and Java is at /usr/bin/java.
Set SERVER_ADDRESS=127.0.0.1 and SERVER_PORT=8080 in the environment file. Add database and API settings there or use a supported secret system.
Restrict environment-file access because it may contain credentials. systemd reads EnvironmentFile and passes its variables to the process; do not publish its contents.
After changing a unit file, reload systemd, enable the service and start it. Inspect service status and journal logs to confirm startup.
A restart loop can indicate a wrong Java version, unavailable database or missing setting. Resolve the logged cause instead of increasing restart frequency.
Public HTTP and TLS
Nginx receives public requests and forwards them to the local application. This is a reverse proxy: clients connect to Nginx, not directly to port 8080.
Configure a server_name for the domain, proxy_pass to http://127.0.0.1:8080, and suitable proxy timeouts and request-size limits.
Forward the original host and protocol where needed. Trust forwarded headers only from the controlled proxy, especially when generating OAuth callback URLs.
Point DNS to the VPS and enable HTTPS with a certificate for that domain. Certificate renewal must remain configured after the initial setup.
Allow the required SSH and public web ports in the firewall while keeping the application port private. Preserve working SSH access when changing remote firewall rules.
Rate limiting can reduce some abusive request patterns. It does not guarantee protection from every denial-of-service attack.
Verify and operate the deployment
Check the local application, the public HTTPS endpoint, certificate validity and an authenticated database operation as separate boundaries.
Keep logs available and manage their retention. Monitor process failures, request errors and resource pressure.
Restart or reboot during a controlled check to confirm service recovery. A green local build does not prove boot-time startup on the server.
Deploy a new artifact with a known rollback path. Database backups and migration planning are separate from JAR replacement.
